topk.text: Speaker, then a system was introduced in this country where it was thought that the country was wasting so much time on education. Some of us could not comprehend what exactly that meant. So, the bottom line was that we have a six-year primary education, a three-year junior secondary school, and then a three-year senior secondary school education. From a period of about 17 years’ pre-university education, we now have a period of basically 12 years’ pre-university education. Mr Speaker, we have shunned off the total by about five years. Five years are completely gone. If we were understudying the developed countries — I take always Britain as my starting point. Mr Speaker, Britain introduced all these things—all the education and all that we do in this country—to us. We are also part of the Commonwealth now. We are part of their colonial past. That is not what is done in Britain, and I always cite the example of the fact that we are taught 67 6th December, 2023 68 Statements in English language. They are taught in English language, but they spend at least 13 years, and that is their language. We have to learn the language of English, yet we have cut back even on the basic education of the English people by a year. They do 13 years and we do 12 years. I have not quite understood the purpose of this. Mr Speaker, the worrying aspect of all of this is that we have also introduced a system which, by the indications I have just given, ensures that everybody ends up at the university. The Hon Member spoke about his room that he went to check later and he found that they were two or whatever. My block was the K Block of the Legon Hall of the University of Ghana. At the time we were in there — We left the university in 1986. In 1982, before we were beaten and sent home by the Provisional National Defence Council (PDNC) Government, we were two. Those who have fond memories of the days, there were two people in a room. When I went back to check, I heard that there were so many people on campus. There was congestion in the classrooms and dormitories. I went in there to check, and in my case, there were 12 female students in my room. The K Block in Legon Hall was always a male block, but when I went, there were about 12 ladies in one room. That is an indication of the issues that we are all grappling with. How did they put 12 people in one room? Mr Speaker, we can talk about the 500 or so students in the classroom. I had gone to check on the Political Science Department one day, and when I went, the lecturer had a megaphone in his hand and I wondered what he was doing. With all respect, it was not a funfair or an outdoor function. It was a lecture hall. I was told that there were about 2,000 students

Dr Forson: Mr Speaker, the Hon Member quoted and made reference to a law that has been repealed by this House. Mr Speaker, he made reference to the Education Act, 2008 (Act 778). I do not know where he is getting his facts from. However, the reference he has made has clearly been repealed. Mr Speaker, on that basis, you have to rule him out. [Interruption] I did not hear him state that. He did not say that. It has been repealed completely. So, I do not know what he is talking about. Mr Speaker, secondly, the Act talks about certificates and not licensure examinations. That is not what the Act talks about. It has been repealed, in any case. Mr Speaker: Hon Minority Leader, he actually stated that it has been repealed but it has been repeated in the new Act that he read. So he said it has been repealed. Dr Armah: Mr Speaker, I thank you very much. Mr Speaker, I introduced that to buttress the point that in the year 2016 when the then Government said that they were going to introduce the licensure regime, the prevailing Act was the Education Act, 2008 (Act 778), and that Act imposed a statutory requirement for teachers to write that licensure examination. So, it could not be the case that they were going to introduce that without the licensure examination. That is why I said that amounted to double standards. Mr Speaker, let me indicate that the entire process is to improve teacher quality. As we speak now, the qualification of Ghanaian teachers has now received international acceptance. When I left the shores of Ghana to go and teach in the United Kingdom (UK), I went through a serious and laborious assessment process. Mr Speaker, as we speak now, because of the licensure regime — The Ghana Teacher and Licensure Examination and Certification, when a Ghanaian teacher moves to the UK now, they are automatically granted Qualified Teacher Status (QTS), which was very difficult to get then. Mr Speaker, this examination is all part of that full package. So, any attempt to try and scrap it would adulterate the quality that has been accepted internationally. Mr Speaker, having said that, if one looks at the Budget Statement, it is very clear about the support structures that are being given to teachers. We are now going to the fifth. 4:21 p.m. Mr Dafeamekpor: Mr Speaker, I am making this intervention on Constitutional grounds. Yesterday, 24th November, 2025, the High Court of Tamale ordered that the outcome of the election—these are very serious matters, that the outcome of the 7th December elections 2024, which brought the Hon Matthew Nyindam to this House, as MP for Kpandai was flawed, and therefore that election has been ordered to be rerun. Mr Speaker, ipso facto, Hon Matthew Nyindam is no longer a Member of this House. He is not. Hear me, so that he can respond. So, by 97 26th November, 2025 98 Government’s Financial Policy, 2026 operation of law, he is no longer a Member of this House with a voice. That is one. Mr Speaker, two, we have received the court orders and received proof of service. The orders of the court have been duly served on Parliament. It was served yesterday. It will serve the Minority to listen to me in silence. If they are minded to respond, then they can do so. Mr Second Deputy Speaker: Hon Members, please, let us listen to him. Mr Dafeamekpor: Mr Speaker, I have a copy of the proof of service of the orders of the Tamale High Court, dated, 24th November, 2025 and served to Parliament. The orders of the court were served by the court bailiff of the High Court, Accra.

Sciences. Mr Speaker, the Government has introduced many measures to boost STEM education not just in the senior high schools; it starts from the basic schools. Basic STEM programmes have been introduced. We want to create an ecosystem of education that is second to none in the world. Mr Speaker, public schools are being transformed. It is not just right that after paying taxes, parents would have to pay for their children to go to private schools because the public schools are not an option. Under Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo and Bawumia’s Government, we are laying a solid foundation for the transformation of public schools. When you drive by and see the East Legon STEM Academy building go up—and it is a public school—it tells you that we mean business. Mr Speaker, we would change the face of public education. We will make sure that my colleagues on the other Side would one day line up in front of a public school to enrol their children. These days, people do not do that; people have run away from our public schools. We want to make sure we reform them so that a lot of people could walk into our public schools. We want to create a public education regime where the son of the parliamentarian would sit in the same class with the son of the labourer to study 125 25th July, 2024 126 Statements — Mid-Year Review, 2024 together and become friends to develop a more united nation. Mr Speaker, when they ask where the money is, the money has been invested in free secondary education. Starting with an enrolment of 800,000 in 2016, today, we have over 1.4 million of our students enrolled in secondary education. That is where the money is. Mr Speaker, my Government was committed to making an investment like none other in the world: a nation where 70 per cent of our students are in boarding school, and it is still free. Look around the world and see where you would find one. It took a bold President who wanted to change the course of history of his country to make that bold commitment to free secondary school education. And within seven to eight years, he has committed the resources to change the course of history of our nation. That is where the money is, and the money would continue to go there, so far as the good people of Ghana do us the honour and give us the privilege to continue beyond the eight— [Interruption] We would change the course of history of our nation. Mr Speaker, the Government is committed to education. The Government is committed to change the course of history of our nation. We would continue to do just that because the future of our nation is better. It is better when we are in government than when we are not in government.
